summary: Specifies the Aggregate Server Access Protocol, which together with ENRP provides a high-availability data transfer mechanism over IP. It uses handle-based addressing, which separates a logical endpoint from its IP addresses, so clients can reach a pool of servers by name. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: ASAP lets a client address a group of servers through one logical handle. It can select a server from the group and try another when the selected server becomes unreachable.

subtitle: Client-facing access, registration, and failover for server pools.

tldr.problem: Applications tied to one server address may lose service when that server or address becomes unavailable.
tldr.mechanism: ASAP uses a logical pool handle, asks an ENRP server for pool members, and selects a member according to the pool's selection policy. It can try another member when one is unreachable.
tldr.outcome: ASAP defines the client-facing protocol for registration, handle resolution, and failover, and works with ENRP. RFC 5352 is Experimental.

today: RFC 5352 is an Experimental RFC published in September 2008. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Pool Handles and Server Roles
sections.content:
The Aggregate Server Access Protocol (ASAP) provides access to a pool of servers that offer the same application function. A pool handle names the pool without binding the client to one server IP address.

ASAP works with the Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP), which keeps pool membership information. The pool contains pool elements (servers) and pool users (clients). ASAP does not share application transaction state between servers, so a failure can still lose a transaction.
sections.plainLanguage: A pool handle names a group of servers rather than one server address. ASAP works with ENRP to find which servers belong to the group.

sections.title: Messages for Registration and Lookup
sections.content:
A pool element sends ASAP_REGISTRATION to its home ENRP server to create a pool or join one. It can later send a deregistration request to leave. A pool user sends ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION to request the list of pool elements for a handle.

The response includes the available pool elements and the selection policy. A client may request updates when pool membership changes. ASAP also defines keep-alive messages, unreachable reports, cookies, business cards, server announcements, and error messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A server registers itself with ENRP, and a client asks ENRP which servers are in a named pool. The response can include the current members and a rule for choosing among them.

sections.title: Registration, Resolution and Failover
sections.content:
A pool element finds a home ENRP server and registers its handle and transport addresses. A client resolves a handle, selects a pool element according to the pool policy, and sends application data directly to that element.

If the selected element becomes unreachable, ASAP can select another element before reporting failure to the sender. A pool element can send a cookie to a client; during failover, the client can present the latest cookie to another element. A business card can provide a preferred failover order.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers register, and clients resolve the pool handle to find members. If one member cannot be reached, the client can try another member and may provide it with a cookie from the earlier connection.

sections.title: Selection Policies and Transport
sections.content:
ASAP separates the logical pool handle from the addresses of its member servers. The pool's selection policy determines which member receives a request; the RFC notes round-robin as the default when a response does not include another overall policy.

ASAP messages between a pool element and ENRP server use SCTP. Messages between a pool user and ENRP server use SCTP or TCP. Application data between a pool user and pool element may use a transport protocol named by the pool element.
sections.plainLanguage: The pool policy determines which server receives a request. Control messages use SCTP for servers registering with ENRP, while client lookup can use SCTP or TCP.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes security mechanisms in conjunction with ENRP and the RSerPool security requirements. ASAP deployments need authenticated communication with ENRP servers, and the RFC identifies TLS as a required-to-implement security mechanism.

The document also requires the protocol to limit certain repeated error and keep-alive messages to reduce flooding risks. The message formats and parameter definitions are specified alongside ENRP in RFC 5354.
sections.plainLanguage: ASAP relies on authenticated, protected communication with ENRP. The RFC also calls for limits on some message types that could otherwise be used in a flood.
